questions.question: Why does Allah address the Prophet in verse 1 by the description 'the one wrapped in his cloak' rather than by his name or the formal title of messenger?
options: A) Because the Prophet's name had not yet been revealed to him at that point
B) To create an intimate, personal address that acknowledged the Prophet's vulnerable human state at that moment
C) Because using the title of messenger would have been premature before the mission officially began
D) To signal that the Prophet should always wear a cloak when receiving revelation
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that calling the Prophet by his physical state rather than a formal title creates a deeply personal address, showing how Allah speaks to His servant in the most tender and direct way possible. The Prophet had sought comfort under his cloak after being overwhelmed by the sight of Jibril, and Allah met him precisely in that moment of vulnerability, demonstrating that divine guidance does not wait for us to compose ourselves before reaching us.

questions.question: True or false: according to the tafsir, the command 'Arise and warn' in verse 2 marks the transition from the Prophet being a private recipient of revelation to a public messenger with a mission to warn all of humanity.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir explains that 'ya ayyuhal muddaththir' marks the definitive transition from the Prophet as a private worshipper to a public messenger. Al-Zuhayli notes that the deliberate gentleness of the address does not soften the weight of the command: the Prophet is being propelled from private spiritual existence into a world-historical role.

questions.question: Which hadith, cited by Ibn Kathir as recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim, provides the historical occasion for the opening of Surah Al-Muddaththir?
options: A) The narration of Aisha describing the very first revelation in the cave of Hira
B) The narration of Jabir ibn Abdullah in which the Prophet describes seeing the angel seated on a throne between the sky and earth, returning home frightened and saying 'Cover me, cover me'
C) The narration of Umar ibn al-Khattab describing the Prophet's first public address to the Quraysh
D) The narration of Abu Bakr about the Prophet receiving the command to establish prayer
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim cites the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim, in which Jabir relates that the Prophet said he was walking, heard a voice, looked up, saw the angel he had seen in Hira sitting on a chair between the sky and earth, was frightened, returned home, and said 'Cover me, cover me,' whereupon Allah revealed these opening verses.

questions.question: Verse 3 commands the Prophet to 'magnify your Lord.' What does the tafsir identify as the significance of this command coming immediately after the call to arise and warn?
options: A) It instructs the Prophet to begin every public address with the phrase Allahu Akbar as a greeting
B) It establishes that the entire prophetic mission must be rooted in the recognition of Allah's greatness before any outward action is taken
C) It restricts the command to warn so that it only applies when the Prophet feels spiritually prepared
D) It implies that magnifying Allah through good deeds can substitute for verbal proclamation of his message
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that before strategic planning, community-building, or public speech, the Prophet is told to root everything in tawthiq of Allah's greatness. Wahbah al-Zuhayli notes that this command establishes Tawhid as the entire foundation, not merely one component, of the prophetic mission. Ibn Uthaymeen adds that dawah is inseparable from aqidah — a call to people that neglects the call to recognise Allah's greatness has inverted the divine priority.

questions.question: True or false: the tafsir describes the command 'be patient for the sake of your Lord' in verse 7 as a form of passive resignation to hardship rather than an active act of worship.
questions.explanation: The tafsir explicitly rejects this reading. Layer 1 states that patience in Islamic teaching is a conscious act of worship — a voluntary turning of the soul toward Allah in the midst of difficulty, not mere endurance. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes this sabr as 'active, energised' spiritual posture, and the particle 'li-rabbika' (for your Lord) is what elevates it from human virtue into an act of divine nearness, as Fakhr al-Din al-Razi observes.

questions.question: Who is described in the hadith cited by Ibn Kathir as already holding the trumpet to his lips, waiting for the divine command — and what did the Prophet tell his companions when they became anxious upon hearing this?
options: A) The angel Jibril; the Prophet told them to seek refuge in the words 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah'
B) The angel Israfil; the Prophet told them to say 'Hasbuna Allah wa niam al-wakil' (Allah is sufficient for us and the best disposer of affairs)
C) The angel Mikail; the Prophet told them their prayers would protect them from fear on that Day
D) An unnamed angel; the Prophet told them only the righteous would hear the trumpet's sound
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim records the hadith in which the Prophet describes the angel Israfil already holding the trumpet to his lips, his forehead bowed forward, waiting for the divine command. When the companions became deeply shaken, the Prophet told them to say 'Hasbuna Allah wa niam al-wakil.' The tafsir notes this vivid image is connected to the trumpet verse of Surah Al-Muddaththir.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir records that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah privately acknowledged the Quran's extraordinary eloquence and power before publicly labelling it as magic.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim records the narration from Qatada in which al-Walid said privately: 'By Allah, I have thought about what this man says and it is not poetry. Verily, it has a sweetness and it is truly elegant. Verily, it is exalted and nothing can overcome it.' Despite this honest private assessment, he turned to the Quraysh and labelled the Quran as sorcery, making his condemnation especially severe because the lie was premeditated and conscious.

questions.question: Saqar is described in verses 26-29. Which of the following accurately reflects what those verses state about it?
options: A) It is a level of Hell reserved only for those who physically persecuted the Prophet during his lifetime in Mecca
B) It leaves nothing unburned and spares nothing, and it scorches and blackens the human skin of those within it
C) Its flames are extinguished and reignited at regular intervals, giving the condemned brief periods of cold
D) It is administered by a single great angel who personally oversees each individual's punishment
questions.explanation: Verse 28 states that Saqar leaves nothing and spares nothing, and verse 29 adds the image 'lawwahah lil-bashar' — scorching and blackening the human skin. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Abbas's explanation that this means 'burning the skin of man,' and al-Qurtubi notes the Arabic verbal form indicates this blackening is continuous and repeated, not a single occurrence.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb observed that al-Walid's two accusation — calling the Quran 'magic' in verse 24 and 'mere human speech' in verse 25 — are logically contradictory. What does Qutb say this reveals about the psychology of rejecting truth?
options: A) That al-Walid was intellectually confused because the Quran's literary style genuinely resembled both magic and poetry simultaneously
B) That the Quraysh were internally divided and al-Walid was awkwardly reporting the views of two different factions

C) That when a person refuses to submit to evidence, counter-arguments need not be consistent — they only need to create distance from the truth, revealing rhetorical sabotage rather than honest engagement
D) That al-Walid retracted the 'magic' accusation and settled on 'human speech' as his final considered verdict
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran writes that the juxtaposition of the two contradictory accusations exposes not just al-Walid's dishonesty but the internal incoherence of all arrogant rejection of truth. Ibn Kathir similarly notes the logical incompatibility, arguing al-Walid wanted to give the Quraysh multiple dismissive labels for different audiences without caring about consistency, since the goal was not to find truth but to provide cover for a decision already made on grounds of pride.

questions.question: True or false: when the number of nineteen guardians of Saqar was revealed in verse 30, Abu Jahl responded with humility, recognizing it as a divine sign beyond human comprehension.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari records the opposite: Abu Jahl responded with contemptuous mockery, declaring before his companions that his people could surely overpower nineteen angel-guardians. This reaction exemplifies exactly what verse 31 then describes — that the number serves as a trial which increases the faith of believers while deepening the arrogance of those whose hearts are diseased.

questions.question: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir identifies verse 31 as unique in the Quran for a particular reason. What is that reason?
options: A) It is the only verse that names a specific angel by rank and number
B) It explicitly lists multiple simultaneous effects of a single divine disclosure, making it a model for how one truth from Allah operates differently according to each heart's receptivity
C) It is the only Meccan verse to address the People of the Book directly by name
D) It contains the longest single sentence in the Quran, making it linguistically exceptional
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir observes that verse 31 is unique in the Quran for explicitly listing the multiple simultaneous outcomes of a single divine disclosure — trial for disbelievers, increased faith for believers, certainty for the People of the Book, and further misguidance for the spiritually diseased — making it a model for understanding how one truth from Allah operates differently depending entirely on the spiritual orientation of the receiver.

questions.question: Verse 38 states 'Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.' The Arabic word 'rahinah' comes from the concept of rahn. What does this metaphor communicate about the soul's relationship to its own deeds?
options: A) That the soul is auctioned off to the highest bidder among the angels based on the total quantity of good deeds
B) That the soul itself is the collateral pledged against its own moral debt and cannot be freed until that debt is settled through repentance and righteous deeds, or faced in divine judgment
C) That souls are collectively pledged as a group, so an entire family can be freed if one righteous member intercedes
D) That the soul is held temporarily in the grave as a pledge until it is redeemed by others' prayers on the Day of Judgment
questions.explanation: The tafsir draws on the ancient Arabian practice of rahn — pledging an item of value as security for a debt. Wahbah al-Zuhayli adds the legal precision that in Islamic jurisprudence a pledged item cannot be reclaimed until the debt is settled, and by analogy the soul cannot be freed from its moral state until purified through sincere repentance and good deeds, or until it faces the divine reckoning. Sayyid Qutb describes this as a profound call to taqwa: life is a mortal pledging of the most precious thing a person possesses, their own soul.

questions.question: True or false: verse 38 rules out intercession entirely, establishing that no soul can benefit from anyone else's prayers or good standing on the Day of Judgment.
questions.explanation: The tafsir is clear that verse 38 establishes the baseline reality of personal accountability without denying that intercession exists. Ibn Uthaymeen explains that the Prophet's intercession for his nation is affirmed, but verse 38 establishes that a soul cannot rely passively on that intercession without itself engaging in repentance and righteous conduct. The verse is a wake-up call, not an abolition of mercy.

questions.question: When the people of Paradise ask the people of Hell 'What put you into Saqar?' in verse 42, al-Tabari records that early scholars understood this question as serving a specific purpose. What purpose did they identify?
options: A) To humiliate the condemned by making them publicly confess in front of the righteous
B) To allow the people of Paradise to petition Allah for clemency on behalf of those they recognise from earthly life
C) To establish the justice of punishment through the condemned's own articulation of their crimes, confirming that divine judgment is fully transparent and causally linked to one's choices
D) To give the condemned a final opportunity to repent before the gates of Hell are permanently sealed
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari records that companions and successors understood this question as one of accountability and disclosure, designed to make the condemned articulate their crimes before the people of Paradise. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi adds that this mirrors the questioning in the grave and affirms that divine justice operates through clear causal links between actions and consequences rather than arbitrary decree. Ibn Kathir notes it reflects Allah's justice: even in punishment, the reasons are made clear.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes the four confessions in verses 43-46 as forming a complete sequence. How does he characterise the relationship between those four confessions?
options: A) He treats the four as independent sins of equal weight with no logical progression between them

B) He argues they form the complete anatomy of spiritual failure: collapse of the relationship with Allah through prayerlessness, then with others through social indifference, then intellectual integrity through vain discourse, and finally belief itself through denial of the Day — a progressive descent
C) He says denial of the Day of Judgment is the only sin that truly matters, with the other three being relatively minor in comparison
D) He focuses on them purely as a historical description of Meccan paganism without drawing wider lessons
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes the four confessions in verses 43-46 as tracing the complete anatomy of spiritual failure: first the collapse of the relationship with Allah through prayerlessness, then the relationship with others through social indifference, then intellectual integrity through vain discourse, and finally belief itself through denial of the Day of Judgment. Wahbah al-Zuhayli similarly notes the four span three domains — the vertical relationship with Allah, the horizontal with humanity, and the domain of fundamental belief — forming a complete moral map of human failure.
